messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Hotel Manager
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Stress: Stress, Workplace: Workplace, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Vignette:
Nadia Haddad is a 51-year-old married hotel manager who came to treatment after months of telling herself that what happened was over and that she should have been able to move on. The event she returns to began during a weekday shift at the hotel, when a strong chemical odor started spreading through a lower corridor near service areas and housekeeping storage. At first it registered as something sharp and wrong in the air, stronger than ordinary cleaning products, the kind of smell that catches in the throat and makes the body react before the mind has caught up. As she moved through the building trying to understand what was happening, the odor intensified. Staff were confused, guests were alarmed, and the atmosphere changed quickly from routine workplace pressure to something that felt dangerous and out of control. Nadia remembers the smell most vividly: harsh, sterile, and invasive, close to the antiseptic scent she now says she cannot tolerate. The confusion of the scene, the urgency in people’s voices, and the sense that the building itself was no longer safe have stayed with her in a way that feels immediate rather than past.

In the weeks afterward, she expected to feel shaken for a while, but instead she found that reminders caught her off guard in very physical ways. When she encountered hospital or antiseptic smells, even briefly, her body reacted before she could reassure herself. Walking past a clinic entrance, catching the disinfectant scent in a restroom, or entering an area of the hotel just after deep cleaning could bring a rush of bodily alarm. She described her heart pounding, her muscles tightening, and a wave of dread that made her want to leave immediately. Because the original exposure happened at work, the hotel itself became more complicated for her. She did not think of it simply as her job anymore. Under stress, especially during busy shifts with complaints, staffing problems, or unexpected maintenance issues, she could feel herself become keyed up in a way that seemed out of proportion even to her. It was not just pressure; it was the sense that something could suddenly go wrong again.

Her daily environment now confronts her with reminders she cannot fully control. As a hotel manager, she is expected to move through guest floors, inspect housekeeping standards, respond to operational problems, and remain composed during moments of disruption. Instead, Nadia has found herself hesitating outside recently sanitized rooms, sending other staff to check areas with strong cleaning smells, or lingering in her office longer than she once would have. She has become acutely alert to loud or unexpected sounds in the building—the crash of a dropped tray, a slammed service door, a sudden alarm, raised voices over a radio. Each one jolts her. She knows these sounds are common in hotel operations, yet she experiences them as if her whole system has been primed for danger. On difficult days, a loud noise in the corridor can leave her shaky and breathless, embarrassed in front of employees she is meant to supervise.

Nadia also describes her nights as increasingly difficult. She lies in bed tired but unable to settle, feeling that she has to stay alert. As she explains it, falling asleep means letting her guard down, and some part of her remains unconvinced that it is safe to do that. She listens for noises in the house and outside, noticing every creak or sudden sound. If something startles her, she feels the same surge through her body that she gets at work. Her husband has noticed that she startles more easily and paces the house late at night, though Nadia tends to minimize it and say she is just not sleepy yet. She has become frustrated by how much energy it takes to get through a normal day after another restless night.

Over time these patterns have narrowed her world. Stress at work now feels less manageable, not because she lacks experience, but because pressure, chemical smells, and sudden noises all seem to land on the same already taut system. She has tried to compensate by becoming more controlled and watchful, but that has made her feel less like herself with staff and at home. What finally brought her to seek help was a recent incident at the hotel when a strong disinfectant smell from a cleaned area, followed by a loud bang from a service cart, left her visibly shaken in front of employees. She was disturbed not only by the intensity of the reaction but by the realization that the workplace she has spent years competently running now feels unpredictable to her. Coming to treatment, Nadia says she wants to be able to sleep without feeling she must keep watch and to walk through her hotel without bracing for the next smell or sound. What frightens her most is the sense that her body still acts as though the danger is happening now.
